content: When determining the appropriate interval for retesting, all relevant factors must be considered. This includes assessing drug resistance to emtricitabine (FTC) and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in those who seroconvert while on PrEP. Countries must establish protocols for managing individuals who acquire HIV while on PrEP, including removing them from PrEP, supplementing TDF/FTC with other antiretroviral drugs for early treatment, and implementing interim approaches aligned with national AIDS treatment policies. Clinicians must carefully evaluate various scenarios they may encounter and determine the best strategies to address these situations in service delivery. Transition mechanisms should also be developed for individuals who choose to stop or are unable to continue PrEP. These individuals must have continued access to other HIV prevention services and risk reduction strategies. Additional data must be gathered to address ethical considerations in resource-limited settings where universal access to treatment has not been achieved. Countries need to assess how to allocate their available resources for HIV prevention effectively, weighing the cost-benefit of PrEP within combination prevention strategies. This evaluation should also consider the social, cultural, and political feasibility of delivering PrEP. Following the publication of the iPrEx trial results in November 2010, the World Health Organization (WHO) convened a consultation in February 2011 to seek external advice on whether and how to proceed. Participants, including experts and WHO staff, agreed that full implementation guidelines could not be developed at that time. However, given the importance of the iPrEx data and the need for implementation guidance, WHO sought approval from its Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) to develop guidance for men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women. Approval was granted in June 2011, and work began immediately. In June 2011, additional evidence emerged from the TDF2 trial and the Partners PrEP trial, the latter of which was stopped early due to overwhelming evidence of effectiveness. WHO then sought and received GRC approval in October 2011 to expand the guidance to include serodiscordant couples. Evidence review for this group began in February 2012, following the release of data from the Partners PrEP trial. Systematic reviews of the evidence, including GRADE tables and reviews of values and preferences, were conducted by Caitlin Kennedy and Virginia Tedrow Fonner of Johns Hopkins University. Methodological advice was provided by Eli Akl of the State University of New York at Buffalo. The WHO Steering Group compiled the review copy and drafted the background text and justification for the guidance. The Guideline Development Group, working via email and telephone, finalized the recommendations. When consensus on wording was not immediately achieved, alternative wordings were proposed and circulated until agreement was reached. The External Review Group reviewed the revised draft and suggested alternative wordings, but overall, they found the recommendations to be appropriate, evidence-based, and clearly worded. Members of the External Review Group included experts such as Pedro Chequer, Mean Chhi Vun, Adeeba Kamarulzaman, Lynn Paxton, and Brian Pazvakavambwa. The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation provided financial support for the development of this guidance. The guidance will be reviewed and revised in 2015, taking into account implementation experiences from various countries. Until then, new evidence on PrEP will be continuously monitored, and any necessary revisions will be communicated directly to countries. The guidance is being published in English, French, and Spanish and disseminated to countries and WHO/UNAIDS staff to support the development of demonstration projects based on this advice. All members of the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group completed WHO declarations of interest forms. Four individuals declared potential conflicts of interest, but these were not deemed significant. For example, one panel member, Carlos Caceres, received travel support from an institution conducting a key study but had no personal benefit from his work on the guidance. Similarly, Lynn Paxton declared that Gilead Sciences provided drugs for a study in Botswana, but no personal benefit resulted. Two others reported professional responsibilities related to PrEP, which were not considered conflicts of interest. The guidance references several key studies and publications, including those by Abdool Karim, Grant, Baeten, Thigpen, and others, which provide evidence on the effectiveness and safety of PrEP in various populations. These studies highlight the importance of PrEP in preventing HIV transmission among MSM, heterosexual men and women, and serodiscordant couples. The guidance also incorporates findings from modeling studies and cost-effectiveness analyses to inform its recommendations.
